Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: Epidemiology & Risk Factors in Gynecologic Cancer
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
Cervical, endometrial, and vulvar cancer are three distinct gynecologic malignancies that share overlapping anatomy but have very different causes, typical patients, and disease biology. Cervical and vulvar cancer are driven mainly by HPV infection, while endometrial cancer is driven mainly by unopposed estrogen exposure: understanding this split explains why screening, prevention, and the typical patient look so different across the three diseases.

Cervical Cancer

Cervical cancer is the 4th most common malignancy in women globally, though incidence in the United States has been steadily decreasing thanks to widespread Pap smear screening and HPV vaccination. The median age at diagnosis is 50 years, with most cases diagnosed between ages 35-44, younger than endometrial cancer, reflecting the fact that HPV infection and the years-long progression through cervical dysplasia typically begins in young adulthood. The most common histology is squamous cell carcinoma.

The dominant risk factor, by a wide margin, is human papillomavirus (HPV), associated with more than 90-95% of cases. HPV subtypes 16 and 18 alone account for roughly 70% of cervical cancers; other oncogenic ("high-risk") strains include 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58. Because HPV is sexually transmitted, several other risk factors cluster around exposure and persistence of infection: young age at first intercourse, multiple sexual partners, and multiparity all increase cumulative HPV exposure or the chance that an infection persists rather than clears. Smoking and immunocompromised states (HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients) impair the immune system's ability to clear HPV infection, allowing progression to dysplasia and cancer. Low socioeconomic status is an important risk factor as well, largely through reduced access to screening. A distinct, non-HPV risk factor is in utero diethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure, which is specifically associated with clear cell carcinoma of the cervix and vagina.

A sobering disparity: SEER data from 2013-2019 show that the death rate from cervical cancer in Black women and Native American women is 65% higher than in white women, a gap driven by disparities in access to screening and timely treatment rather than biology alone.

Because HPV is the causal agent, cervical cancer is uniquely preventable through vaccination and screening. The 9-valent HPV vaccine is recommended for children ages 11-12, with catch-up vaccination through age 26; adults 27-45 may be vaccinated based on shared decision-making. Critically, vaccination status does not change screening recommendations, a vaccinated patient still needs routine cytology/HPV testing. The USPSTF screening guidelines are age-stratified: ages 21-29 get cervical cytology alone every 3 years; ages 30-65 can choose cytology alone every 3 years, hrHPV testing alone every 5 years, or co-testing (cytology + hrHPV) every 5 years; and patients over 65 with an adequate history of negative screening (3 negative Paps or 2 negative co-tests in a row, no history of moderate/severe dysplasia) can stop screening altogether.

Clinical Pearl HPV vaccination prevents infection but does not treat or reverse existing infection, that is why vaccinated patients still require age-appropriate cervical cancer screening for life (until they meet criteria to stop).

Endometrial Cancer

Endometrial cancer is the most common gynecologic malignancy in the United States, accounting for roughly 3.6% of all cancers. Unlike cervical cancer, it is a disease of later life: the median age at diagnosis is 63, and it is uncommon under age 45 (about 6% of cases). The most common histology is adenocarcinoma.

The central risk factor is unopposed estrogen: estrogen exposure that is not balanced by progestin. Progestin normally counteracts estrogen's proliferative effect on the endometrium; without it, the endometrium is chronically stimulated toward hyperplasia and, eventually, carcinoma. This single unifying mechanism explains a whole list of risk factors that might otherwise look unrelated:

  • Physiologic sources of excess estrogen exposure: obesity (peripheral fat converts androgens to estrogen), nulliparity, early menarche, and late menopause, all of which increase lifetime estrogen exposure.
  • Pathologic associations: diabetes mellitus and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), both of which involve chronic anovulation and unopposed estrogen.
  • Exogenous exposure: unopposed estrogen replacement therapy (without a progestin) and tamoxifen, which acts as an estrogen agonist on the endometrium even as it blocks estrogen receptors in breast tissue.

A separate, non-estrogen pathway is genetic: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC, hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer), an autosomal dominant condition caused by mismatch repair (MMR) gene mutations, confers a 30-70% lifetime risk of endometrial cancer compared to about 3% in the general population. Any patient diagnosed with endometrial cancer under age 50 should prompt consideration of Lynch syndrome screening, and known MMR carriers may be counseled toward prophylactic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy once childbearing is complete.

Racial disparities in endometrial cancer differ from cervical cancer: incidence is roughly equal between Black and white women, but Black women with endometrial cancer have higher mortality. This is explained partly by a higher incidence of aggressive (type II/serous) histology in Black women, and partly by ongoing disparities in access to timely cancer care.

Clinical Pearl Complex atypical hyperplasia carries a 30-40% risk of concurrent or progressive malignancy (versus only ~3% for complex hyperplasia without atypia), this distinction is why atypia on endometrial biopsy usually prompts surgical staging rather than watchful waiting.

Vulvar Cancer

Vulvar cancer is rare, about 5% of gynecologic cancers and 0.7% of all cancers, giving U.S. women roughly a 1-in-333 lifetime chance of diagnosis. Risk rises with age, peaking in the 7th decade of life. The most common histology, as with cervical cancer, is squamous cell carcinoma.

Vulvar cancer has two distinct etiologic pathways, which is a useful way to organize the risk factors:

  • HPV-dependent pathway: driven by the same oncogenic HPV strains as cervical cancer (16, 18, 33), progressing through vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN). VIN III carries an 80% risk of progression to invasive cancer if untreated.
  • HPV-independent pathway: arises from chronic vulvar dystrophies, most notably lichen sclerosus, which carries roughly a 5% risk of malignant transformation. This pathway tends to affect older women and is not related to sexual history or HPV exposure.

Recognizing which pathway is at play matters clinically, an HPV-driven lesion in a younger patient with a VIN history behaves differently than a lichen sclerosus–associated cancer in an elderly patient, though both funnel into the same staging and treatment framework.

Anatomy & Lymphatics.title: Pelvic Anatomy & Lymphatic Drainage
Anatomy & Lymphatics.html:
Where a gynecologic cancer is anatomically located, and which lymph nodes it drains to, is not academic trivia, it is the single biggest determinant of how radiation fields are designed. This section walks through the anatomy of the cervix, uterus, and vulva, and then the lymphatic pathways that connect each organ to specific, predictable nodal stations.

Cervix and Uterus

The cervix is the lower, cylindrical portion of the uterus. Its inner canal (the endocervical canal) is lined by columnar epithelium, while the outer surface (the ectocervix) is lined by squamous epithelium. The point where these two epithelial types meet, the squamocolumnar junction, located at the external os, is the single most common site for cervical carcinogenesis, because it is a zone of active cellular transformation that is especially vulnerable to HPV-driven dysplasia.

The uterus as a whole is divided into the cervix and lower uterine segment (lower third) and the body/fundus (upper two-thirds). Within the uterine wall, three layers matter for different reasons: the endometrium is the site of origin for endometrial cancers, the myometrium is where uterine sarcomas arise (and the layer whose depth of invasion determines endometrial cancer staging), and the serosa is the outer covering whose breach defines more advanced disease.

Three ligaments anchor the uterus and cervix and serve as literal conduits for local tumor spread and lymphatic drainage:

  • The cardinal ligament attaches the cervix to the pelvic sidewall.
  • The broad ligament attaches the uterus to the pelvic sidewall.
  • The uterosacral ligament attaches the lower uterus to the sacrum.

Parametria refers to the connective tissue surrounding the uterus/cervix carried within these ligaments, parametrial invasion is a key staging and surgical-candidacy checkpoint in cervical cancer. The adnexa refers to the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and broad ligaments together.

Lymphatic Drainage: Cervical and Endometrial Cancer

Because the cardinal, broad, and uterosacral ligaments physically carry the lymphatic channels away from the cervix and uterus, tumor cells traveling through these ligaments predictably arrive at the same nodal stations that receive normal pelvic lymphatic drainage. For cervical cancer, this means regional lymphatic drainage to the presacral, obturator, internal and external iliac, common iliac, and paraaortic nodes. Distant metastatic sites include the lungs, liver, and bone; supraclavicular lymph nodes can also become involved via the thoracic duct. This is precisely why the standard pelvic radiation field for cervical cancer is designed to encompass the obturator, internal/external iliac, and common iliac nodal chains, the field follows the anatomy of the drainage.

For endometrial cancer, the regional lymphatic stations are very similar: bilateral parametrial nodes, obturator, internal and external iliac, common iliac, presacral/sacral, and paraaortic nodes. One important exception: lesions arising at the uterine fundus can drain directly to the paraaortic nodes, bypassing the pelvic chain entirely, though this is uncommon. This possibility is part of why paraaortic nodal assessment is considered during surgical staging of endometrial cancer, particularly for fundal tumors.

Clinical Pearl The squamocolumnar junction sits at the external os and is the classic site where cervical dysplasia and carcinoma begin, it is also the anatomic landmark used to define brachytherapy Point A and Point B during treatment planning.

Vulva and Inguinofemoral Drainage

The vulva includes the mons pubis, clitoris, and labia majora/minora, the great majority of vulvar cancers (over 70%) arise on the labia, with 10-15% arising on the clitoris. Bartholin's glands sit in the posterior labia majora and are rarely the primary site of malignancy. The fourchette is the point where the labia minora merge posteriorly.

Vulvar lymphatic drainage follows a stepwise, superficial-to-deep pathway: superficial inguinal nodes → deep inguinal (femoral) nodes → external iliac nodes → pelvic chain, traveling along channels that run with the femoral vein. The risk of nodal involvement rises in proportion to tumor thickness. Critically, pelvic lymph nodes are considered distant/metastatic disease in vulvar cancer staging, not regional disease, reflecting how far the tumor must travel through the inguinofemoral stations before reaching the pelvis. One structural exception is worth remembering: clitoral lesions can drain directly to pelvic nodes, bypassing the inguinal stations, because of the clitoris's distinct embryologic and lymphatic origin.

This inguinal-to-pelvic anatomic continuity is exactly why, when groin (inguinofemoral) nodes are positive, radiation fields are frequently extended upward to cover the pelvis as well, the disease has a direct anatomic conduit to spread there next.

Clinical Pearl In vulvar cancer, a clitoral or midline lesion can drain to contralateral or even direct pelvic nodes, this is part of why well-lateralized tumors (more than 2 cm from midline) are the only candidates for unilateral sentinel lymph node biopsy.

Workup & Staging.title: Workup & FIGO Staging
Workup & Staging.html:
All three gynecologic cancers are staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, but each cancer's staging is built around a different anatomic question: how deep into the cervical stroma, how deep into the myometrium, or how far from the vulva. Workup is aimed squarely at answering that question before treatment begins.

Cervical Cancer

Cervical cancer is often asymptomatic and picked up on routine screening. When symptomatic, patients may report abnormal vaginal discharge, post-coital bleeding, dyspareunia, or pelvic pain.

Workup begins with a history and physical exam focused on gynecologic history, with a pelvic and abdominal exam that specifically includes palpation of the supraclavicular and inguinal lymph nodes (reflecting the distant spread pattern described above). Labs include CBC, CMP, and consideration of HIV testing and a pregnancy test. Tissue diagnosis starts with colposcopy and cervical biopsy (often via LEEP); if the biopsy is inadequate, a cold knife cone (CKC) biopsy is performed, and notably, this can serve as definitive treatment in truly early-stage disease. For more advanced disease or suspected bladder/rectal extension, exam under anesthesia (EUA) with cystoscopy and rectosigmoidoscopy is added, and a ureteral stent may be needed. Imaging is split by purpose: pelvic MRI with and without contrast (plus vaginal gel) delineates the local extent of disease, while PET/CT is used for nodal and distant staging. Older imaging modalities (CXR, barium enema, skeletal x-ray, and intravenous pyelogram) remain technically allowed by FIGO but are largely historical.

The 2018 FIGO staging system for cervical cancer is built around depth of stromal invasion and tumor size (Stage I), extension beyond the uterus (Stage II), and involvement of the lower vagina, pelvic sidewall, or lymph nodes (Stage III):

StageDefinition
IA1Stromal invasion ≤3 mm depth
IA2Stromal invasion >3 and ≤5 mm depth
IB1≥5 mm stromal invasion, tumor <2 cm
IB2Tumor >2 and ≤4 cm
IB3Tumor >4 cm
IIAExtends beyond uterus, upper vagina, no parametria (IIA1 ≤4cm, IIA2 >4cm)
IIBInvades parametria, not to pelvic wall
IIIALower 1/3 vagina, no pelvic sidewall extension
IIIBPelvic sidewall extension or hydronephrosis/non-functioning kidney
IIIC1 / IIIC2Pelvic node metastasis (C1) / paraaortic node metastasis (C2)
IVA / IVBAdjacent organ invasion (bladder/bowel) / distant metastasis

The 2018 revision was notable for adding nodal status directly into the stage (IIIC1/IIIC2) for the first time, a lymph-node-positive patient is now automatically at least Stage III regardless of local tumor extent, reflecting how strongly nodal disease predicts outcome.

Clinical Pearl A cold-knife cone biopsy is not just diagnostic, in truly microinvasive disease (IA1), it can be definitive therapy, sparing the patient a hysterectomy entirely.

Endometrial Cancer

The classic presentation is postmenopausal vaginal bleeding, seen in about 90% of cases, which is why any postmenopausal bleeding triggers an endometrial cancer workup until proven otherwise. Other, less specific symptoms include abdominal/pelvic pain, distension, urinary or rectal bleeding, and constipation. A history of endometrial hyperplasia or atypia is an important clue: complex hyperplasia without atypia carries roughly a 3% risk of malignancy, while complex atypia carries a 30-40% risk.

Workup starts with a complete H&P and pelvic exam, with consideration of CBC, LFTs, and CA-125. Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) assesses the endometrial stripe thickness; an abnormally thickened stripe prompts biopsy, typically under hysteroscopic guidance, with dilation and curettage (D&C) reserved for a nondiagnostic biopsy. Unlike cervical cancer, endometrial cancer workup pivots heavily on surgical staging: hysterectomy itself is often the key staging procedure, and further imaging is guided by the surgical stage that results. When imaging is used, MRI with and without contrast assesses local extent, PET/CT detects nodal involvement, and CXR or CT chest (or full CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for high-grade tumors) screens for distant metastasis.

Endometrial cancer staging has evolved: the 2009/2017 FIGO system was based purely on anatomic extent (myometrial invasion depth, cervical involvement, extrauterine spread), while the newer 2023 FIGO system incorporates histology, grade, and LVSI status directly into the stage, reflecting how strongly these biologic factors affect prognosis independent of anatomic extent.

Stage (2017)Definition
IALimited to endometrium or <50% myometrial invasion
IB≥50% myometrial invasion
IIInvades cervical stroma, no extrauterine extension
IIIASerosal and/or adnexal invasion
IIIBVaginal or parametrial invasion
IIIC1 / IIIC2Pelvic node involvement / paraaortic node involvement
IVA / IVBBladder/bowel mucosal invasion / distant metastasis

The key discriminator between IA and IB is 50% myometrial invasion: this single measurement is the most testable, management-relevant number in endometrial cancer staging (more in the Imaging section).

Vulvar Cancer

Vulvar cancer classically presents as an erythematous, ulcerated lesion, sometimes with bleeding or pruritus; groin nodes may be palpable or ulcerated at presentation. Roughly 20% of patients present with a synchronous cervical cancer: a reminder that both cancers share HPV as a cause and screening for one should prompt attention to the other. The lung is the most common site of distant metastasis.

Workup includes H&P with pelvic and rectal exam, labs as indicated (CBC, LFTs, pregnancy test), and biopsy with HPV testing. MRI of the pelvis with and without contrast assesses local extent and groin nodes; PET/CT is considered for clinically advanced disease. The differential diagnosis for a vulvar lesion is broad and includes epidermal inclusion cyst, Bartholin gland disorder, lichen sclerosus, condyloma acuminata, lentigo, acrochordons, and seborrheic keratoses, underscoring why biopsy confirmation is essential before treatment.

The 2021 FIGO staging system for vulvar cancer is built around tumor size/depth of invasion, extension to adjacent structures, and nodal burden:

StageDefinition
IATumor ≤2 cm, stromal invasion ≤1 mm
IBTumor >2 cm, or stromal invasion >1 mm
IIExtension to lower 1/3 urethra, vagina, or anus; nodes negative
IIIAExtension to upper 2/3 urethra/vagina/anus, or regional node ≤5 mm
IIIBRegional lymph node >5 mm
IIICRegional lymph node with extracapsular extension (ECE)
IVA / IVBFixed to bone or fixed/ulcerated node / distant metastasis (includes pelvic nodes)
Clinical Pearl In vulvar cancer, unlike cervical or endometrial cancer, positive pelvic lymph nodes are classified as Stage IVB, distant disease, not a regional nodal substage, which reflects how far tumor cells must travel (through the entire inguinofemoral chain) before reaching the pelvis.

Imaging.title: Imaging in Gynecologic Cancer
Imaging.html:
Imaging plays a different, well-defined role for each of the three cancers, but the common thread is that MRI is the workhorse for local (T-stage) assessment in all three, while PET/CT is the workhorse for nodal and distant staging. Knowing exactly what question each modality is answering is the key to using them correctly.

Cervical Cancer

MRI is the imaging modality of choice for local staging of cervical cancer, and its importance is formalized in the 2018 FIGO staging system, which explicitly incorporates imaging findings. The standard protocol uses high-resolution T2-weighted imaging in three planes oriented orthogonal to the cervical long axis (2-4 mm slices), plus an axial T1 large-field-of-view sequence extending to the renal hila to screen for adenopathy along the paraaortic chain.

The single most important MRI pearl in cervical cancer imaging: an intact, hypointense T2 cervical stromal ring is a strong negative predictor of parametrial invasion. Because parametrial invasion is what pushes a tumor out of surgical candidacy and into the definitive chemoradiation pathway, this one imaging sign often distinguishes surgical candidates from chemoRT candidates. The coronal plane best depicts parametrial extension when the ring is in question.

Vaginal extent on MRI directly determines cervical cancer substage: involvement of the upper two-thirds of the vagina corresponds to Stage IIA, while involvement of the lower third corresponds to Stage IIIA. Pelvic sidewall invasion (Stage IIIB) is suggested when tumor is within 3 mm of, or abutting, the obturator internus, levator ani, piriformis, or iliac vessels; hydronephrosis is another signal of Stage IIIB disease. As a general rule, tumors greater than 4 cm are not amenable to primary radical surgery. MRI is also excellent at excluding bladder or rectal invasion: posterior bladder wall thickening or mucosal disruption argues for bladder invasion, while loss of the posterior perirectal fat plane argues for rectal invasion.

PET/CT's primary role in cervical cancer is different, it is used for nodal (pelvic/paraaortic) and distant metastatic staging, not local tumor assessment, since MRI's superior soft-tissue contrast makes it better suited to evaluating the primary tumor and parametria.

Clinical Pearl On cervical cancer MRI, "coronal plane, intact ring, no parametrial invasion" is the imaging shorthand for a surgical candidate, memorize that the coronal sequence is specifically the best plane for evaluating the parametria.

Endometrial Cancer

MRI is likewise the modality of choice for endometrial cancer, but here its chief job is measuring depth of myometrial invasion: the pivotal FIGO discriminator between Stage IA (<50% invasion) and Stage IB (≥50% invasion) under the 2023 FIGO system, which also folds in histology, grade, and LVSI status. Cervical stromal invasion, when present, upstages disease to Stage II. Beyond that, Stage III reflects serosal/adnexal spread (IIIA), vaginal/parametrial spread (IIIB), or pelvic/paraaortic nodal spread (IIIC), while Stage IV reflects bladder/bowel mucosal invasion or distant metastasis.

This is worth emphasizing because it is arguably the single most testable imaging concept in endometrial cancer: an accurate measurement of myometrial invasion depth directly changes management, it informs the extent of lymphadenectomy performed at surgery and the subsequent decision about adjuvant radiation. Getting the <50% vs. ≥50% call right is not an academic exercise; it changes what the surgeon does and what the radiation oncologist recommends afterward.

Vulvar Cancer

Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (roughly 80-85% of cases, peak age 65-70, often arising from a VIN precursor) shows low-to-intermediate T1 signal and intermediate-to-high T2 signal on MRI, which is roughly 80% accurate for assessing local lesion size and extent. Beyond the primary lesion, MRI is also used to evaluate the groin (inguinal/femoral) lymph nodes: this is a critical role, since inguinofemoral node status is the single strongest driver of both prognosis and radiation field design in vulvar cancer (recall from the Anatomy section that positive groin nodes can necessitate extending fields to cover the pelvis). FIGO staging for vulvar cancer follows the general pattern of Stage 0 (carcinoma in situ), Stage I (confined to the organ), Stage II (local invasion of adjacent structures), Stage III (regional nodal or local spread), and Stage IV (distant metastases, which specifically includes positive pelvic nodes).

Clinical Pearl For endometrial cancer, remember the imaging-to-management chain in one sentence: MRI measures myometrial invasion depth → depth determines FIGO stage → stage drives extent of lymphadenectomy and the adjuvant RT decision.

Treatment Paradigms.title: Treatment Paradigms Across Gynecologic Cancer
Treatment Paradigms.html:
Despite arising from different tissues, all three cancers follow a similar logical structure: assess whether the disease is confined enough for surgery alone, and if not, or if surgery reveals high-risk features, layer on radiation, with or without chemotherapy, based on well-defined criteria. This section walks through each cancer's decision tree.

Cervical Cancer

  • Early-stage (IA1, IA2, IB1, IB2, IIA1: generally <4cm, no parametrial involvement), fertility-sparing → cold knife cone (CKC) excision, or radical trachelectomy
  • Early-stage, not pursuing fertility preservation, <5mm invasion (Stage IA) → Type II (modified radical) hysterectomy
  • Stage IB1 and above → Type III (radical) hysterectomy, removing the parametria out to the pelvic sidewall/sacrum
  • Meets Sedlis criteria (2 of 3: LVSI, deep stromal invasion, tumor size ≥4cm) → adjuvant RT alone, 45–50.4 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions
  • Meets Peters criteria (any 1 of 3: positive margins, positive nodes, parametrial involvement) → adjuvant chemoRT (RT + weekly cisplatin 40 mg/m²)
  • Close (<5mm) or positive vaginal margin → add a vaginal cuff brachytherapy boost, 5 Gy x2 fractions
  • Locally advanced (IB3, IIA2–IVA) → definitive concurrent chemoradiation + brachytherapy boost, no surgery: pelvic RT 45 Gy/25 fx (SIB to 55–57.5 Gy for involved nodes) + weekly cisplatin, then brachytherapy to an HR CTV D90 of 85–90 Gy (cumulative EQD2)
  • Any definitive treatment → keep overall treatment time ≤8 weeks (no more than 56 days); each day beyond 8 weeks costs roughly 0.5–1% local control
Clinical Pearl Sedlis = radiation alone (structural/pathologic risk factors: LVSI, deep invasion, size); Peters = chemoRT (higher-risk factors that predict systemic as well as local failure: positive margins, positive nodes, parametrial invasion). Peters criteria are "worse" findings, which is why they earn concurrent chemotherapy on top of radiation.

Endometrial Cancer

  • Operable disease → surgical staging: hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (Class I for early-stage; Class II/III for gross cervical involvement) ± omental/peritoneal biopsies for high-risk disease; SLNB has largely replaced full lymphadenectomy for lower-risk cases
  • Low risk → observation
  • High-intermediate risk (age ≥60 + focal LVSI, or similar) → vaginal brachytherapy (VBT): 21 Gy/3 fx to 5mm depth alone, or 10 Gy/2 fx as a boost after pelvic RT
  • High risk (substantial LVSI, or high-risk histology: clear cell, serous, carcinosarcoma, mixed, undifferentiated) → pelvic RT ± VBT boost
  • Locally advanced (Stage III–IVA) → sequential chemo → EBRT → brachytherapy boost, or concurrent chemoradiation → adjuvant chemotherapy (PORTEC-3, GOG-258)
  • Surgically inoperable (extensive local disease) → preoperative EBRT ± chemo → brachytherapy → surgery, to allow a less extensive (simple rather than radical) hysterectomy
  • Medically inoperable, Stage IA grade 1–2, <4cm → brachytherapy alone
  • Medically inoperable, grade 3 or Stage IB and above → EBRT + brachytherapy boost

Vulvar Cancer

  • VIN → local excision, skinning vulvectomy, imiquimod, topical 5-FU, or laser ablation
  • Stage IA (invasion ≤1mm, negative margins, no other risk factors) → wide local excision alone, no adjuvant treatment needed
  • Stage IB–II → radical local resection or modified radical vulvectomy + inguinal SLNB (can be unilateral if the primary is well-lateralized, >2cm from midline)
  • Margins <8mm → adjuvant RT to the vulva
  • ≥2 positive nodes, or extracapsular extension → adjuvant RT to the inguinal and pelvic nodes
  • Stage III–IVA, resectable → surgical resection preferred
  • Stage III–IVA, unresectable → neoadjuvant chemoradiation with concurrent weekly cisplatin, then biopsy confirmation of response or organ-sparing surgery
  • Sentinel node positive with only micrometastatic disease → inguinal radiation can substitute for full lymphadenectomy
Clinical Pearl Across all three cancers, the goal of upfront surgical selection is the same: operate on patients unlikely to need adjuvant radiation, because combining modalities (surgery + RT ± chemo) reliably increases toxicity without a proportional gain in outcomes compared to choosing one definitive modality up front.

High-Yield Literature.title: High-Yield Literature in Gynecologic Radiation Oncology
High-Yield Literature.html:
The gynecologic cancer literature is unusually rich in practice-defining, named trials, several of the criteria and dosing regimens used every day in clinic trace directly back to a single landmark study. This section walks through the trials that actually changed practice, organized by clinical question, with an emphasis on cervical cancer (where the evidence base is deepest) and condensed coverage of the key endometrial and vulvar trials.

Cervical Cancer, Postoperative Management

GOG 92 (Sedlis et al., 1999; Rotman et al., 2006) enrolled 299 patients with Stage IB cervical cancer and pathologic risk factors after radical hysterectomy and pelvic lymph node dissection, randomizing them to observation versus adjuvant pelvic EBRT (46 Gy/23 fx or 50.4 Gy/28 fx, no vaginal brachytherapy). Radiation produced a significant local recurrence and PFS benefit, 12-year local recurrence fell from 31% to 18%, and 12-year PFS improved from 65% to 78%, but did not significantly improve overall survival (71% vs. 80%, p=0.074). This trial established the Sedlis criteria (need 2 of 3: LVSI; deep stromal invasion of the middle or deep third; tumor size ≥4 cm) as the indication for adjuvant RT alone.

GOG 109 (Peters et al., 2000; Monk et al., 2005) randomized 243 patients with Stage IA2, IB, or IIA cervical cancer after radical hysterectomy, all with at least one high-risk feature (positive margin, positive nodes, or parametrial involvement), to pelvic EBRT alone (49.3 Gy/29 fx) versus the same EBRT plus concurrent and adjuvant cisplatin/5-FU chemotherapy. Adding chemotherapy significantly improved both 4-year PFS (63% → 80%) and 4-year OS (71% → 81%). This trial established the Peters criteria (positive margin, positive nodes, or parametrial involvement) as the indication for adjuvant chemoRT rather than RT alone, notably, unlike GOG 92, this trial showed a genuine OS benefit, reflecting how much higher-risk this population was.

Clinical Pearl GOG 92 (Sedlis) showed a PFS but not OS benefit for RT alone; GOG 109 (Peters) showed both a PFS and OS benefit for adding chemotherapy. The magnitude of benefit tracks the risk level of the population, this is why Peters-criteria patients are treated more aggressively.

Cervical Cancer, Definitive Management

GOG 123 (Keys et al., NEJM 1999) randomized 369 patients with bulky (>4 cm, Stage IB3+) cervical cancer to EBRT alone (45 Gy plus an LDR brachytherapy boost) versus the same EBRT/brachytherapy with concurrent weekly cisplatin (40 mg/m², up to 6 cycles), all patients then underwent extrafascial hysterectomy afterward. Concurrent cisplatin significantly improved both PFS (60% → 71%) and OS (64% → 78%). This trial firmly established that concurrent chemoradiation improves outcomes in the definitive setting.

GOG 71 (Keys et al., 2003) then asked whether the adjuvant hysterectomy used in GOG 123 was actually necessary: 256 patients with tumors >4 cm were randomized to definitive RT alone (EBRT + brachytherapy boost) versus RT followed by extrafascial hysterectomy. There was no significant improvement in OS or PFS with added hysterectomy (OS 58% vs. 56%; PFS 62% vs. 53%, p=0.09). The takeaway, adjuvant hysterectomy does not improve outcomes after definitive chemoRT, is why trimodality therapy (surgery plus definitive chemoRT) is no longer pursued; a patient who has completed definitive chemoRT does not need a subsequent hysterectomy.

GOG 120 (Rose et al., NEJM 1999) addressed which chemotherapy regimen to use, randomizing 575 patients with Stage IIB-IVA cervical cancer receiving RT to concurrent weekly cisplatin alone, versus hydroxyurea alone, versus cisplatin + 5-FU + hydroxyurea. Hydroxyurea alone performed worse; both cisplatin-containing arms performed similarly. This established weekly cisplatin 40 mg/m² as the standard concurrent chemotherapy regimen, the simplest effective option won out.

OUTBACK (Mileshkin et al., Lancet Oncol 2023) tested whether adding chemotherapy after chemoRT (rather than the more established question of chemotherapy during RT) would help: 926 patients receiving definitive cisplatin-based chemoRT (including brachytherapy boost) were randomized to no further treatment versus adjuvant carboplatin/paclitaxel every 3 weeks for 4 cycles. There was no improvement in 5-year PFS (61% vs. 63%) or OS (71% vs. 72%). The clear message: adjuvant chemotherapy after definitive chemoRT does not add benefit: the concurrent chemoRT backbone from GOG 120/123 remains standard, without additional adjuvant systemic therapy tacked on afterward.

Clinical Pearl Four trials, one coherent story for locally advanced cervical cancer: concurrent cisplatin during RT helps (GOG 123), cisplatin alone is the right regimen (GOG 120), adjuvant hysterectomy afterward doesn't help (GOG 71), and adjuvant chemotherapy afterward doesn't help either (OUTBACK). Definitive chemoRT with brachytherapy boost is a complete, self-sufficient treatment.

Cervical Cancer, Brachytherapy Dosing and the EMBRACE Studies

The EMBRACE series established the modern, MRI-guided approach to brachytherapy dosing. RetroEMBRACE (Tanderup et al., 2016) established the dose-volume relationship for tumor control probability: a target HR CTV D90 of at least 85 Gy (EQD2) yields local control of 94% for a 20cc tumor, 93% for a 30cc tumor, and 86% for a 70cc tumor, larger tumors need proportionally more dose (roughly +5 Gy per +10cc of volume for equivalent control), and each week of treatment prolongation beyond 7 weeks costs another ~5 Gy of equivalent dose. This is the origin of the recommended 49-day (7-week) total treatment time.

EMBRACE I (Pötter et al., Lancet Oncol 2021) was a prospective cohort of 1,416 patients treated with MRI-guided adaptive brachytherapy, achieving 92% 5-year local control with 7% G3-5 toxicity. Long-term follow-up analyses from this cohort produced two more practice-defining findings: (1) an EBRT dose of 50 Gy produced worse late GI toxicity than 45 Gy with no local control benefit (3-year G2+ diarrhea 9.5% with 45 Gy vs. 19.9% with 50 Gy), establishing 45 Gy/25 fx as the standard EBRT dose; and (2) adenocarcinoma histology showed worse local control than squamous cell carcinoma at the same dose (95% vs. 86% 3-year LC at HR CTV D90 85 Gy), suggesting adenocarcinoma may warrant a higher brachytherapy boost.

EMBRACE II is the prospective validation study in the IMRT/image-guided adaptive brachytherapy (IGABT) era, with detailed DVH constraints, and is also investigating prophylactic paraaortic nodal irradiation in patients with pelvic node-positive disease. Related retrospective data (Vargo 2014, Nomden 2019) show that paraaortic failure is low (~2.5%) when only pelvic nodes are involved, but rises with common iliac node involvement, three or more positive nodes, or bulky nodes, many practices now favor prophylactic paraaortic RT in these higher-risk subsets.

Standard brachytherapy boost fractionation schemes (Viswanathan et al., 2012), delivered after 45 Gy pelvic EBRT with concurrent cisplatin, include 5.5 Gy x 5 (for residual disease ≤4 cm), 6 Gy x 5 (for >4 cm), 5 Gy x 6, or 7 Gy x 4, all designed so the cumulative EQD2 to HR CTV D90 reaches at least 85 Gy.

Finally, RTOG 1203/TIME-C (Klopp et al., JCO 2018) compared 3D-conformal RT to IMRT in 278 patients with cervical or endometrial cancer receiving pelvic radiation. IMRT significantly reduced patient-reported GI and GU toxicity, even though clinician-reported adverse events showed no significant difference, highlighting that clinicians tend to under-report toxicity compared to patients themselves. This trial is why IMRT is the preferred modality for pelvic radiation in gynecologic cancer.

Clinical Pearl The EMBRACE studies converge on one number worth memorizing: HR CTV D90 ≥85 Gy (EQD2) is the brachytherapy dose target, achieved through 45 Gy EBRT plus a brachytherapy boost, completed within roughly 7 weeks total treatment time.

Endometrial Cancer, Key Trials

The nodal-risk framework begins with GOG 33 (Creasman et al., 1987), a prospective observational study showing that grade and depth of myometrial invasion predict lymph node metastasis risk, risk is under 5% for endometrium-only disease, roughly 5-10% for inner/middle-third invasion, and rises with outer-third invasion depending on grade (roughly 10% for grade 1, 20% for grade 2, 30% for grade 3). Whether lymphadenectomy actually improves outcomes was then tested by the ASTEC trial and the Italian trial (Benedetti et al.), both of which found no significant OS or DFS benefit to lymphadenectomy over observation, lymphadenectomy helps with staging information but does not itself improve outcomes. The FIRES study (Rossi et al., Lancet 2017) then validated sentinel lymph node biopsy as an alternative: in 385 patients with clinical Stage I disease, SLNB had 97.2% sensitivity and 99.6% negative predictive value for detecting nodal metastasis, establishing that SLNB can safely replace full pelvic/paraaortic lymphadenectomy in early-stage disease.

For adjuvant treatment of intermediate-risk disease, two trials define modern practice. GOG 99 (Keys et al., 2004) randomized 392 women with intermediate-risk features (grade 2-3, LVSI, outer-third myometrial invasion) to observation versus whole pelvic RT (50.4 Gy/28 fx) after full surgical staging, finding that RT reduced 2-year recurrence (12% → 3% overall; 26% → 6% in the high-intermediate-risk subgroup) without an OS benefit, at the cost of worse GI, GU, and hematologic toxicity. PORTEC-1 (Creutzberg et al., 2011) asked a similar question in 714 patients without required lymphadenectomy, finding that postoperative whole-pelvis RT significantly reduced 15-year locoregional recurrence (16% → 6%), again driven by the high-intermediate-risk subgroup, without an OS benefit. In both trials, roughly 75% of recurrences occurred at the vaginal vault, raising the question of whether vaginal brachytherapy alone could achieve the same local benefit with less toxicity.

PORTEC-2 (Nout et al., Lancet 2010) answered that question directly: 427 high-intermediate-risk patients were randomized to whole pelvic RT versus vaginal brachytherapy (VBT) alone. There was no difference in local recurrence, DFS, distant metastasis, or OS between arms (though pelvic recurrence was slightly higher with VBT), while VBT caused significantly less GI/GU toxicity. This established that VBT alone is sufficient for high-intermediate-risk disease, sparing many patients the toxicity of whole pelvic radiation. The Swedish low-risk study (Sorbe et al., 2009) completed the risk-adapted picture by showing no significant benefit to adding VBT in truly low-risk disease (<50% myometrial invasion, grade 1-2), supporting observation alone for this group.

For locally advanced/high-risk disease, PORTEC-3 (de Boer et al., Lancet 2018) randomized 660 high-risk patients to RT alone versus RT with concurrent and adjuvant chemotherapy, finding a 5-year OS and failure-free survival benefit with chemotherapy (76% → 81%) driven specifically by Stage III disease and serous histology, with significantly worse acute and late toxicity as the tradeoff. GOG 258 (Matei et al., NEJM 2019) compared chemotherapy alone to chemoradiation in 736 Stage III-IVA patients, finding no difference in RFS overall, though chemoradiation produced significantly less vaginal and pelvic recurrence at the cost of significantly more distant metastases (likely reflecting a delay in effective systemic therapy). Together, these trials support a modern approach of adjuvant chemotherapy for distant control combined with radiation for local/pelvic control in high-risk disease.

Finally, immunotherapy has entered advanced/recurrent endometrial cancer: both the RUBY trial (dostarlimab) and NRG GY018 (pembrolizumab) showed that adding a PD-1 inhibitor to carboplatin/paclitaxel significantly prolongs PFS in Stage III-IV or recurrent disease, with particularly striking benefit in mismatch-repair-deficient (dMMR) tumors, though benefit was also seen in mismatch-repair-proficient (pMMR) tumors.

Vulvar Cancer, Key Trials

For nodal management, GOG 88 (Stehman et al., 1992) directly compared inguinofemoral lymph node dissection to inguinal RT alone in node-negative patients and closed early because the RT arm performed significantly worse (PFS 90% vs. 65%; groin recurrence 18% vs. 0%), establishing that surgical groin dissection is superior to inguinal RT alone as initial management (the RT arm was later criticized for underdosing the groin). The GROINSS-V studies then refined how to select patients for dissection at all: GROINSS-V (van der Zee et al., 2008) showed that patients with a negative sentinel lymph node have very low groin recurrence (2.3% at 5 years) when full lymphadenectomy is omitted, and GOG 173 (Levenback et al., 2012) confirmed SLNB's reliability as an alternative to full dissection, with a false-negative predictive value of just 2% for tumors under 4 cm.

For patients with a positive sentinel node, GROINSS-V-II/GOG 270 (Oonk et al., JCO 2021) tested whether radiation could replace full lymphadenectomy: for sentinel node micrometastases (≤2 mm), adjuvant RT alone produced a low 2-year groin recurrence rate of 1.6%, supporting RT as a safe alternative to surgery. However, for sentinel node macrometastases, RT alone had a substantially higher recurrence rate than lymphadenectomy (22% vs. 7%), meaning full lymphadenectomy (or the ongoing GROINSS-V-III/NRG GY024 trial testing concurrent chemoRT) remains preferred for macrometastatic disease.

For the question of adjuvant radiation to positive nodes, GOG 37 (Kunos et al., 2009) randomized node-positive patients after radical vulvectomy and bilateral groin dissection to further groin surgery versus bilateral pelvic and groin RT, finding that RT significantly improved outcomes specifically in patients with ≥2 positive nodes, extracapsular extension, or fixed/ulcerated nodes (2-year groin recurrence 24% vs. 5%; OS benefit in the high-risk subgroup), this is the origin of the ≥2 positive nodes/ECE indication for adjuvant pelvic and inguinal RT. A supporting SEER analysis (Parthasarathy et al., 2006) suggested adjuvant RT may also benefit patients with a single positive node, particularly when fewer than 12 nodes were removed.

For locally advanced, unresectable disease, GOG 101 (Moore et al., 1998) established that preoperative split-course chemoRT (5-FU/cisplatin) achieves high resectability (~95%) prior to surgery, and GOG 205 (Moore et al., 2012) improved on this with continuous-course chemoRT to a higher dose (57.6 Gy/32 fx) with weekly cisplatin, achieving higher response rates (64% clinical complete response, 50% pathologic complete response) with acceptable toxicity, demonstrating that avoiding the treatment break of split-course RT improves outcomes, consistent with the total-treatment-time principle seen in cervical cancer.

Clinical Pearl The vulvar nodal literature builds a clean decision ladder: SLNB first (GOG 173) → observe if negative (GROINSS-V) → RT alone is enough for micrometastatic positive nodes (GROINSS-V-II) → but macrometastatic or high-risk positive nodes (≥2 nodes, ECE, fixed/ulcerated) need full dissection plus adjuvant pelvic/groin RT (GOG 37).
